title: Chapter 14. Of the First and Second Natural Laws, and of Contracts
paragraphs: The RIGHT OF NATURE, which writers commonly call Jus Naturale, is the liberty each man has to use his own power as he himself wills, for the preservation of his own nature — that is, of his own life — and consequently of doing anything which, in his own judgment and reason, he conceives to be the aptest means to it.

By LIBERTY is understood, according to the proper meaning of the word, the absence of external impediments. These impediments may often take away part of a man's power to do what he would, but they cannot hinder him from using the power left to him according as his judgment and reason direct.

A LAW OF NATURE (Lex Naturalis) is a precept or general rule, found out by reason, by which a man is forbidden to do what is destructive of his life, or what takes away the means of preserving it, and to omit that by which he thinks it may be best preserved. Those who write on this subject usually confuse Jus and Lex — Right and Law — yet they ought to be distinguished. For RIGHT consists in the liberty to do or to forbear, whereas LAW determines and binds to one of these. So Law and Right differ as much as obligation and liberty, which in one and the same matter are inconsistent.

And because the condition of man (as has been declared in the previous chapter) is a condition of war of everyone against everyone — in which everyone is governed by his own reason, and there is nothing he can use that may not be a help in preserving his life against his enemies — it follows that in such a condition every man has a right to everything, even to one another's body. And therefore, as long as this natural right of every man to everything endures, there can be no security for any man (however strong or wise he may be) of living out the time which nature ordinarily allows men to live.

And consequently it is a precept, or general rule of reason, “That every man, ought to endeavour Peace, as farre as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek, and use, all helps, and advantages of Warre.” The first branch of this rule contains the first and fundamental law of nature, which is: “To seek Peace, and follow it.” The second contains the sum of the right of nature, which is: “By all means we can, to defend our selves.”

From this fundamental law of nature, by which men are commanded to endeavor peace, is derived this second law: “That a man be willing, when others are so too, as farre-forth, as for Peace, and defence of himselfe he shall think it necessary, to lay down this right to all things; and be contented with so much liberty against other men, as he would allow other men against himselfe.” For as long as every man holds this right — of doing anything he likes — so long are all men in the condition of war. But if other men will not lay down their right as well as he, then there is no reason for anyone to divest himself of his, for that would be exposing himself to prey (which no man is bound to do) rather than disposing himself toward peace. This is that law of the Gospel: “Whatsoever you require that others should do to you, that do ye to them.” And that law of all men: “Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris” (Do not do to another what you would not want done to you).

To LAY DOWN a man's right to anything is to divest himself of the liberty of hindering another from the benefit of his own right to the same. For he who renounces or passes away his right does not give to any other man a right which that other did not have before — because there is nothing to which every man did not have a right by nature — but only steps out of the other's way, so that the other may enjoy his own original right without hindrance from him (though not without hindrance from another). So the effect that accrues to one man from another's relinquishing his right is just so much diminution of impediments to the use of his own original right.

A right is laid aside either by simply renouncing it, or by transferring it to another. By simply RENOUNCING it, when a man does not care to whom the benefit of it accrues. By TRANSFERRING it, when he intends the benefit to some particular person or persons. And when a man has in either manner abandoned or granted away his right, he is then said to be OBLIGED, or BOUND, not to hinder those to whom such right is granted or abandoned from the benefit of it; and to do so is his DUTY, not to make void that voluntary act of his own. Any such hindrance is INJUSTICE, and INJURY, as being Sine Jure (without right) — the right having been previously renounced or transferred. So injury or injustice, in the controversies of the world, is somewhat like what in the disputations of scholars is called absurdity. For just as it is called an absurdity there to contradict what one maintained at the beginning, so in the world it is called injustice and injury voluntarily to undo what from the beginning one had voluntarily done. The way by which a man either simply renounces or transfers his right is a declaration, or signification, by some voluntary and sufficient sign or signs, that he does so renounce or transfer, or has so renounced or transferred it, to the person who accepts it. And these signs are either words only, or actions only, or (as most often happens) both words and actions. They are the BONDS by which men are bound and obliged: bonds that have their strength not from their own nature (for nothing is more easily broken than a man's word), but from fear of some evil consequence on the rupture.

Whenever a man transfers his right or renounces it, it is either in consideration of some right reciprocally transferred to him, or for some other good he hopes for by it. For it is a voluntary act, and the object of every voluntary act of a man is some good to himself. And therefore there are some rights which no man can be understood, by any words or other signs, to have abandoned or transferred. First, a man cannot lay down the right to resist those who assault him by force to take away his life, because he cannot be understood to aim by this at any good to himself. The same may be said of wounds, chains, and imprisonment — both because there is no benefit following from such patience (as there is from the patience of letting another be wounded or imprisoned), and because a man cannot tell, when he sees men proceed against him by violence, whether they intend his death or not. And lastly, the motive and end for which this renouncing and transferring of right is introduced is nothing else but the security of a man's person — in his life, and in the means of preserving life so as not to be weary of it. And therefore if a man by words or other signs seems to despoil himself of the end for which those signs were intended, he is not to be understood as if he meant it, or that it was his will, but that he was ignorant of how such words and actions were to be interpreted.
The mutual transferring of right is what men call CONTRACT.

There is a difference between transferring the right to the thing and transferring (or tradition, that is, delivery of) the thing itself. For the thing may be delivered together with the transfer of the right — as in buying and selling for ready money, or in the exchange of goods or lands — and it may be delivered some time afterward.

Again, one of the contractors may deliver the thing contracted for on his part, and leave the other to perform his part at some specified later time, being meanwhile trusted; and then the contract on his part is called PACT, or COVENANT. Or both parties may contract now, to perform hereafter; in which cases the one who is to perform in the time to come, being trusted, his performance is called keeping of promise, or faith; and the failure to perform (if it is voluntary) is called violation of faith.

When the transferring of right is not mutual, but one of the parties transfers in hope of gaining by it friendship or service from another (or from his friends), or in hope of gaining the reputation of charity or magnanimity, or to free his mind from the pain of compassion, or in hope of reward in heaven — this is not contract, but GIFT, FREE-GIFT, GRACE: words that signify one and the same thing.

Signs of contract are either express, or by inference. Express, when they are words spoken with understanding of what they mean. Such words are either of present or past time — as “I give, I grant, I have given, I have granted, I will that this be yours” — or of the future, as “I will give, I will grant.” Words of the future are called Promise.

Signs by inference are sometimes the consequence of words, sometimes of silence, sometimes of actions, sometimes of forbearing an action. Generally, a sign by inference of any contract is whatever sufficiently shows the will of the contractor.

Words alone, if they are of time to come and contain a bare promise, are an insufficient sign of a free gift, and therefore not binding. For if they are of the future, like “Tomorrow I will give,” they are a sign that I have not given yet — and consequently that my right is not transferred, but remains until I transfer it by some other act. But if the words are of present or past time, such as “I have given, or do give, to be delivered tomorrow,” then my tomorrow's right is given away today; and that by the force of the words, even if there were no other indication of my will. There is a great difference in the meaning of these words: Volo hoc tuum esse cras, and Cras dabo — that is, between “I will that this be thine tomorrow,” and “I will give it to thee tomorrow.” The phrase “I will,” in the former, signifies an act of the will present; in the latter, it signifies a promise of an act of the will to come. So the former words, being of the present, transfer a future right; the latter, being of the future, transfer nothing. But if there are other signs of the will to transfer a right besides words, then, even though the gift is free, the right may be understood to pass by words of the future. For example, if a man offers a prize to whoever comes first to the end of a race, the gift is free; and though the words are of the future, the right still passes — for if he had not wanted his words to be so understood, he should not have let the race run.

[Signs Of Contract Are Words Both Of The Past, Present, And Future.] In contracts, the right passes not only where the words are of present or past time, but also where they are of the future. For all contract is mutual transfer, or exchange, of right; and therefore one who promises only because he has already received the benefit for which he promises is to be understood as intending the right to pass. For unless he had been content to have his words so understood, the other party would not have performed his part first. For this reason, in buying and selling and in other contractual acts, a promise is equivalent to a covenant, and therefore binding.

He who performs first in a contract is said to MERIT what he is to receive by the performance of the other; and he has it as due. Likewise when a prize is offered to many, to be given only to the one who wins, or when money is thrown among many to be enjoyed by those who catch it, although this is a free gift, yet so to win or so to catch is to merit, and to have it as DUE. For the right is transferred in the offering of the prize and in the throwing of the money, though it is not determined to whom — that is decided only by the outcome of the contest. But between these two kinds of merit there is this difference: in contract, I merit by virtue of my own power and the contractor's need; in this case of free gift, I am enabled to merit only by the kindness of the giver. In contract, I merit at the contractor's hand that he should part with his right; in this case of gift, I do not merit that the giver should part with his right, but that, once he has parted with it, it should be mine rather than another's. And this I think is the meaning of that distinction in the schools between Meritum Congrui and Meritum Condigni. For God Almighty, having promised paradise to those men (hoodwinked with carnal desires) who can walk through this world according to the precepts and limits prescribed by him, they say that whoever so walks shall merit paradise Ex Congruo. But because no man can demand a right to paradise by his own righteousness or any other power in himself, but only by the free grace of God, they say no man can merit paradise Ex Condigno. This, I say, I think is the meaning of that distinction; but since disputers do not agree on the meaning of their own terms of art any longer than it serves their turn, I will not affirm anything of their meaning. Only this I say: when a gift is given indefinitely, like a prize to be contended for, he who wins merits, and may claim the prize as due.

If a covenant is made in which neither of the parties performs at once, but they trust one another, then in the condition of mere nature (which is a condition of war of every man against every man) it is void upon any reasonable suspicion. But if there is a common power set over them both, with right and force sufficient to compel performance, it is not void. For he who performs first has no assurance that the other will perform afterward, because the bonds of words are too weak to bridle men's ambition, avarice, anger, and other passions, without the fear of some coercive power; and in the condition of mere nature, where all men are equal and judges of the justness of their own fears, no such coercive power can possibly be supposed. And therefore he who performs first only betrays himself to his enemy, contrary to that right (which he can never abandon) of defending his life and his means of living.

But in a civil state, where there is a power set up to constrain those who would otherwise break faith, that fear is no longer reasonable; and for this reason, he who by the covenant is to perform first is obliged to do so.

The cause of fear that makes such a covenant invalid must always be something that arises after the covenant is made — some new fact or other sign of the will not to perform; otherwise it cannot make the covenant void. For what could not hinder a man from promising ought not to be admitted as a hindrance to performing.

He who transfers any right transfers the means of enjoying it, so far as lies in his power. So a man who sells land is understood to transfer the herbage and whatever grows upon it; nor can the seller of a mill turn away the stream that drives it. And those who give a man the right of government in sovereignty are understood to give him the right of levying money to maintain soldiers and of appointing magistrates for the administration of justice.

To make a covenant with brute beasts is impossible, because not understanding our speech they understand nothing of and accept no transfer of right, nor can they transfer any right to another; and without mutual acceptance there is no covenant.

To make a covenant with God is impossible except by the mediation of such people as God speaks to — either by supernatural revelation, or by his lieutenants who govern under him and in his name — for otherwise we do not know whether our covenants are accepted or not. And therefore those who vow anything contrary to any law of nature vow in vain, as being a thing unjust to pay such a vow. And if the thing is commanded by the law of nature, it is not the vow but the law that binds them.

The matter, or subject, of a covenant is always something that falls under deliberation (since to covenant is an act of the will — that is, an act, and the last act, of deliberation), and is therefore always understood to be something to come, and judged possible by the one who covenants to perform.

And therefore, to promise what is known to be impossible is no covenant. But if what was thought possible later proves impossible, the covenant is valid and binds — not to the thing itself, yet to its value; or, if that too is impossible, to the unfeigned endeavor of performing as much as is possible. For no man can be obliged to more.

Men are freed from their covenants in two ways: by performance, or by being forgiven. For performance is the natural end of obligation; and forgiveness is the restoration of liberty, being a retransferring of that right in which the obligation consisted.

Covenants entered into through fear, in the condition of mere nature, are binding. For example, if I covenant to pay a ransom or render service for my life to an enemy, I am bound by it. For it is a contract in which one receives the benefit of life, while the other is to receive money or service for it; and consequently, where no other law (as is the case in mere nature) forbids the performance, the covenant is valid. Therefore prisoners of war, if they are trusted with the payment of their ransom, are obliged to pay it; and if a weaker prince makes a disadvantageous peace with a stronger out of fear, he is bound to keep it — unless (as has been said before) some new and just cause of fear arises to renew the war. And even in commonwealths, if I am forced to redeem myself from a thief by promising him money, I am bound to pay it, until the civil law discharges me. For whatever I may lawfully do without obligation, I may lawfully covenant to do through fear; and what I lawfully covenant, I cannot lawfully break.

An earlier covenant voids a later one. For a man who has passed away his right to one person today does not have it to pass to another tomorrow; and therefore the later promise transfers no right, but is null.

A covenant not to defend myself from force by force is always void. For (as I have shown before) no man can transfer or lay down his right to save himself from death, wounds, and imprisonment — the avoidance of which is the only end of laying down any right. And therefore the promise of not resisting force, in any covenant, transfers no right, nor is binding. For although a man may covenant thus: “Unless I do so, or so, kill me,” he cannot covenant thus: “Unless I do so, or so, I will not resist you when you come to kill me.” For man by nature chooses the lesser evil, which is the danger of death in resisting, rather than the greater, which is certain and present death in not resisting. And this is granted to be true by all men, in that they lead criminals to execution and prison with armed men, even though such criminals have consented to the law by which they are condemned.

A covenant to accuse oneself, without assurance of pardon, is likewise invalid. For in the condition of nature, where every man is judge, there is no place for accusation; and in the civil state, accusation is followed by punishment, which being force, a man is not obliged not to resist. The same is also true of the accusation of those by whose condemnation a man falls into misery — such as a father, wife, or benefactor. For the testimony of such an accuser, if it is not willingly given, is presumed to be corrupted by nature, and therefore not to be received; and where a man's testimony is not to be credited, he is not bound to give it. Likewise, accusations under torture are not to be reckoned as testimony. For torture is to be used only as a means of guesswork and light in the further examination and search for truth; and what is confessed under it tends to the relief of the one being tortured, not to the informing of the torturers. It therefore ought not to have the credit of sufficient testimony — for whether he delivers himself by true accusation or false, he does so by the right of preserving his own life.

Since the force of words (as I have noted before) is too weak to hold men to the performance of their covenants, there are in man's nature only two imaginable helps to strengthen it. These are either a fear of the consequences of breaking one's word, or a glory or pride in appearing not to need to break it. The latter is a generosity too rarely found to be relied on, especially in the pursuers of wealth, command, or sensual pleasure, who make up the greatest part of mankind. The passion to be reckoned upon is fear; of which there are two very general objects: one, the power of spirits invisible; the other, the power of those men one will offend by breaking faith. Of these two, though the former is the greater power, the fear of the latter is commonly the greater fear. The fear of the former is in every man his own religion, which has its place in the nature of man before civil society. The latter does not — at least not enough place to keep men to their promises, because in the condition of mere nature the inequality of power is not perceived but by the outcome of battle. So before the time of civil society, or in its interruption by war, there is nothing that can strengthen a covenant of peace agreed upon against the temptations of avarice, ambition, lust, or other strong desire, but the fear of that invisible power which each one worships as God, and fears as an avenger of their treachery. All therefore that can be done between two men not subject to civil power is to put one another to swear by the God he fears. This swearing, or OATH, is a form of speech, added to a promise, by which the one who promises signifies that, unless he performs, he renounces the mercy of his God, or calls upon him for vengeance on himself. Such was the heathen form: “Let Jupiter kill me else, as I kill this Beast.” So is our form: “I shall do thus, and thus, so help me God.” And this, with the rites and ceremonies each one uses in his own religion, so that the fear of breaking faith might be the greater.

From this it appears that an oath taken according to any form or rite other than that of the one who swears is in vain, and no oath. And there is no swearing by anything that the swearer does not think is God. For although men have sometimes used to swear by their kings, out of fear or flattery, they would thereby have it understood that they attributed divine honor to them. And swearing unnecessarily by God is just profaning his name; and swearing by other things, as men do in common talk, is not swearing but an impious custom, picked up from too much vehemence in talking.

It also appears that the oath adds nothing to the obligation. For a covenant, if lawful, binds in the sight of God without the oath as much as with it; if unlawful, it does not bind at all, even though confirmed by an oath.
